claims.statement: Clomiphene citrate (Clomid) is FDA-approved for the treatment of ovulatory dysfunction in women desiring pregnancy; it is not approved, and the label states there is no adequate evidence of effectiveness, for male infertility.

context.population: women with ovulatory dysfunction desiring pregnancy
context.doseText: Label regimen: 50 mg daily for 5 days as an initial course; a second course of 100 mg daily for 5 days may be used if ovulation does not occur (label text, not a use recommendation).

claims.statement: Clomiphene citrate is a triphenylethylene selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) that competes with estrogen at estrogen-receptor-binding sites in the hypothalamus and pituitary, triggering increased pituitary gonadotropin (FSH/LH) release that drives follicular development and a preovulatory gonadotropin surge.

claims.statement: Clomiphene citrate labeling carries warnings for ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), which can progress rapidly and in severe cases has resulted in death from hypovolemic shock, hemoconcentration, or thromboembolism; for visual disturbances (blurring, spots, flashes) that may occasionally be irreversible, especially at increased dosage — an independent systematic review characterizes the specific link between clomiphene and central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) as a possible predisposing association for which further controlled trials are needed, not an established causal relationship; and for an increased chance of multiple pregnancy.

context.population: women treated with clomiphene citrate for ovulation induction

extractedEvidence.quote: may progress rapidly (within 24 hours to several days)
gross ovarian enlargement, gastrointestinal symptoms, ascites, dyspnea, oliguria, and pleural effusion
Blurring or other visual symptoms such as spots or flashes may occasionally occur during therapy...visual disturbances may be irreversible, especially with increased dosage.
There is an increased chance of multiple pregnancy
CC may predispose to CRVO, but further trials are clearly needed in this area.
Physicians should be aware of the potential risk of CC, especially in patients with associated risk factors for CRVO.

claims.statement: In a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, clomiphene/enclomiphene (SERM) therapy significantly raised total testosterone versus placebo (moderate-quality GRADE evidence) and was comparable to topical testosterone gel for raising total testosterone; sperm concentration improved more than with testosterone gel, but SERM therapy was not significantly different from placebo on sperm concentration. This off-label male-hypogonadism use is not an FDA-approved indication. Testosterone gains are not shown to persist after discontinuation: an independent primary study of late-onset hypogonadism reported mean total testosterone fell from 22.7±8.1 nmol/L on-treatment to 10.2±3.9 nmol/L three months after stopping clomiphene (p<0.01), with 78% of patients dropping below the 11 nmol/L therapeutic threshold.

claims.statement: Clomiphene ('Clomid') is widely marketed and used off-label as post-cycle therapy (PCT) to restore natural testosterone after anabolic-androgenic steroid use, with vendor content claiming it 'safely' boosts testosterone production; however, the same vendor content and the underlying literature acknowledge that PCT efficacy and the long-term safety of SERM-based PCT protocols remain unsettled. A 2026 dual-centre cohort study (not a randomized controlled trial) reported higher normozoospermia rates at 12 months with clomiphene plus hCG (87.5%) and clomiphene alone (69.2%) versus no treatment (58.6%), and a separate 2026 narrative review still characterizes clomiphene PCT as evidentially unsettled with diagnostic and monitoring challenges; no randomized controlled trial establishes PCT-specific efficacy or safety outcomes, so the vendor's 'safely' framing remains unsupported by controlled trial-grade evidence (as distinct from the FDA-approved female indication or the studied off-label male-hypogonadism use above).

context.population: anabolic-androgenic steroid users seeking to restore endogenous testosterone
context.useCase: post-cycle therapy (PCT) after anabolic steroid use

conflicts.summary: The FDA label states there are no adequate or well-controlled studies demonstrating effectiveness in male infertility and clomiphene is not approved for men, while a published RCT meta-analysis shows a significant testosterone-raising effect in male hypogonadism and vendor/consumer marketing presents off-label PCT use as a 'safe' testosterone-restoration protocol; the strength and applicability of male-use evidence therefore differs sharply by claim (regulatory status vs. hypogonadism RCT data vs. unproven PCT-specific marketing claims) and needs continued human review to keep these distinctions clear to readers.

reviewReasons: Expansion-batch evidence packet requires human review before publication.

Remediation pass 2026-08-29: CAS (50-41-9, verified via a live-fetched Sigma-Aldrich product page and cross-checked against DrugBank/LGC/MedKoo listings), UNII (1B8447E7YI, verified via the live DailyMed label page), and DrugBank salt ID (DBSALT000490, verified via a live-fetched DrugBank page) are now populated. RxNorm and ChEMBL remain unresolved: an RxNav RxCUI lookup returned ambiguous candidate CUIs (142431, 2596) without a confirmable label match this session, and no ChEMBL ID was located; both remain gated pending a follow-up lookup.

Remediation pass 2026-08-29: male-hypogonadism efficacy claim updated with an independent-source durability caveat (mean TT fell from 22.7±8.1 to 10.2±3.9 nmol/L three months post-discontinuation, p<0.01; 78% dropped below the 11 nmol/L threshold), sourced to a live-fetched primary study (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27622282) per the reviewer's finding. Still recommend reconfirming against an endocrine-society guideline at next review.

Remediation pass 2026-08-29: OHSS/visual-disturbance warning claim's CRVO-specific wording softened to 'possible predisposing association, further trials needed', sourced to a live-fetched independent systematic review (karger.com/goi/article/71/2/73/152291), per the reviewer's finding.

Remediation pass 2026-08-29: PCT evidence-gap claim updated with two newly published 2026 independent sources fetched this session (BJU International dual-centre cohort study, PMID 41147237; Andrology narrative review, PMID 42387872) that post-date the packet's original 'no controlled human trials' line. Both are non-randomized/narrative, not RCTs, so the underlying gap (no RCT-grade PCT-specific efficacy or safety data; vendor 'safely' claim unsupported) still holds and the claim remains review-gated; recommend obtaining full-text methodology (PubMed access was blocked by a CAPTCHA this session) at next review.

Remediation pass 2026-08-29 (process fix): removed self-certifying inline reviewFlags language on the adverse-effects claim that had asserted its own completed independent search inline. That search context is recorded here instead: DailyMed CLOMID label ADVERSE REACTIONS section and an FDA.gov safety-communication search were checked and do not address male-hypogonadism-specific adverse-event rates; no regulator document exists for this off-label population, so the claim remains sourced to the peer-reviewed meta-analysis only and stays outside fieldAuthorityRequired scope per the directive.

Male-hypogonadism and PCT-specific evidence is comparatively thin (meta-analysis flags its own safety analysis as underpowered; PCT-specific data is now a non-randomized cohort study, not an RCT) and should be reconfirmed against additional independent source families (e.g., an endocrine society guideline) at review time.
Vendor/marketing source (ro.co) is a single non-independent example of PCT marketing language; broader marketing-claim sampling recommended before publication.
